blocks.text: Quick verdict

SOAX is a strong NetNut replacement for rotating residential and mobile work: 155M residential and 33M mobile IPs on one balance, ISP-level targeting on every plan, SOCKS5, UDP and QUIC, and Scale plans with ASN and ZIP targeting for ad verification. It is not a replacement for NetNut's static ISP proxies, because SOAX no longer sells ISP or datacenter products. Also budget for its credit model: US traffic costs $3/GB on Builder, and credits expire 60 days after purchase.

SOAX and NetNut both ran large residential networks aimed at ad-verification and data teams. Since the FBI seized NetNut's domains in July 2026, after Google tied its residential pool to the Popa botnet, former NetNut customers have been weighing SOAX as a replacement. SOAX brings a large residential and mobile pool and granular targeting, but it also discontinued its own ISP and datacenter proxies in 2025-2026, which matters for anyone who used NetNut's static IPs. This page covers both sides.
What happened to NetNut?

NetNut stopped being a normal buying option on July 2, 2026. That day the FBI and IRS Criminal Investigation seized NetNut-related domains, and Google published research linking the network's residential exit nodes to the Popa botnet, which it estimated at two million or more hijacked home devices. NetNut's parent, Alarum Technologies, rejects the allegations, but its main domains went on to show seizure banners and its share price fell sharply. Whatever the final legal outcome, routing business traffic through that infrastructure now carries legal and reputational risk.

blocks.text: SOAX in 2026: what you get

SOAX rebuilt its pricing in 2026 around credits and country tiers. Residential and mobile traffic share one balance and one per-GB rate, and the rate depends on your plan and the country your exit IP is in: US and German traffic costs more than Indian or Filipino traffic. SOAX advertises 155 million residential and 33 million mobile IPs in 195 countries, supports UDP and QUIC as well as SOCKS5, and includes city and ISP targeting on every plan. It discontinued its datacenter and ISP proxies between late 2025 and mid 2026.

SOAX is a residential and mobile specialist known for granular filtering. Its 2026 pricing replaced fixed GB bundles with plans (Sandbox, Builder, Team, Scale, Enterprise) that include credits, and the credit burn rate depends on the exit country's tier. That makes SOAX cheap for some geographies and expensive for low-volume US work. The network is large (155M residential, 33M mobile advertised) and supports protocols few competitors offer, including UDP and QUIC.

Strengths: Residential and mobile on one balance; UDP and QUIC support alongside SOCKS5; Large pool with city and ISP targeting on every plan; Cheap traffic for Tier 2 and Tier 3 countries. Weak spots: Credits expire after 60 days; US traffic is expensive on small plans; Datacenter and ISP proxies were discontinued.
What NetNut offered, and how SOAX compares

Before the seizure, NetNut was best known for ISP-sourced static residential proxies and a fast rotating residential network aimed at scraping, ad verification and brand-protection teams. Its residential rates generally ran from about $1.87 to $3.53 per GB on larger plans, with higher effective prices on entry plans. SOAX covers much of the same ground: residential and mobile on one balance; scraping apis and unblocker (datacenter and isp discontinued) sit alongside its residential network, which advertises 155M residential + 33M mobile IPs in 195 countries.
What former NetNut customers need, and whether SOAX delivers

Most NetNut accounts were built around three things: static ISP IPs for long-lived sessions, rotating residential traffic with US state and city targeting, and high concurrency for scraping. On static ISP-style IPs, SOAX's answer is no, because it discontinued its ISP and datacenter proxies; its other products are residential and mobile on one balance; scraping APIs and unblocker (datacenter and ISP discontinued). On rotating residential targeting, SOAX offers country, region, city and ISP; ASN and ZIP on Scale plans in 195 countries, with rotating or sticky; mobile sessions up to 60 minutes. On billing, SOAX uses prepaid credits; rate depends on plan and exit-country tier, and unused traffic is handled as follows: credits expire 60 days after they are added. Map each of your old NetNut zones to one of these before you migrate, so nothing breaks on the day you switch.
SOAX pricing

SOAX bills prepaid credits. For US (Tier 1) traffic, the no-fee Sandbox plan costs $5/GB, Builder ($200/month) $3/GB, Team ($500/month) $2.20/GB, and Scale ($1,500/month) $1.50/GB; cheaper countries cost less (Tier 3 from $2/GB on Sandbox). Credits expire 60 days after purchase, and SOAX counts traffic in both directions.

Quick cost check for SOAX: 10 GB comes to $50 on Sandbox (US traffic), and 100 GB comes to $300 on Builder ($200/month plan, $3/GB US). NetNut's larger plans used to run about $1.87-$3.53/GB, so compare against what you actually paid rather than NetNut's headline rate.
How to migrate from NetNut to SOAX

1. Export your NetNut usage history and list the countries, cities and session types you actually used, so you can map them to SOAX's targeting (country, region, city and ISP; ASN and ZIP on Scale plans).
2. Test before you commit. SOAX's testing option: paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99. Run your real targets for a day on the smallest purchase before moving production traffic.
3. Swap the gateway host and credentials in your scraper or browser profiles. SOAX supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5, UDP, QUIC.
4. Compare success rate, response time and cost per successful request against your old NetNut baseline, then move traffic over in stages.
5. Remove any NetNut SDKs, browser extensions or endpoints from your systems, and rotate any credentials that were stored alongside them.
Where SOAX fits best
General web scraping: strong fit. Why: a large pool and its own error headers help debugging.
SERP and rank tracking: strong fit. Why: city and ISP targeting for local results.
Social media and multi-account management: strong fit. Why: mobile IPs on the same balance as residential.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: strong fit. Why: granular location filters.
Ad verification and geo-testing: strong fit. Why: ISP, ASN and carrier-level targeting.
Tight budgets: workable. Why: cheap in Tier 3 countries but pricey for small US jobs.
Protocols and sessions

SOAX supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5, UDP, QUIC and offers rotating or sticky; mobile sessions up to 60 minutes. Targeting covers country, region, city and ISP; ASN and ZIP on Scale plans across 195 countries. Like NetNut's residential gateway, it works through a single backconnect endpoint with location and session options passed in the username, plus IP whitelisting.
How to vet a residential proxy provider after NetNut

The NetNut case showed that a residential pool can look like a normal enterprise product while resting on devices whose owners never meaningfully agreed to share their connection. Before you move traffic to any provider, including SOAX, ask a few direct questions and keep the answers on file:
How are residential IPs sourced? Look for an opt-in SDK or app programme with clear user
consent and compensation, and ask which partner apps are involved.
Does the provider publish an ethics or sourcing policy, and has it been audited or certified (for
example AppEsteem or ISO 27001)?
What KYC does the provider apply to customers, and which target categories are restricted?
Strict onboarding is a good sign, not an inconvenience.
How does it handle abuse reports, and is there a named legal entity and jurisdiction behind the
service?
Can you get contractual assurances, such as a data-processing agreement, if your compliance
team needs them?
Bottom line

NetNut is no longer a provider you can plan around, so the real decision is which network replaces it. SOAX is strongest for mobile-first work such as app testing and social platforms and teams targeting cheaper Tier 2/3 countries, starts at $5/GB on the no-fee Sandbox plan (US, Tier 1), and offers paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99. Test it on your own targets for a day, compare cost per successful request with your old NetNut baseline, and move production traffic in stages.
